summary: Michigan's Lake Huron light at the tip of the thumb: a brick tower of 1857, keepers from a widow in 1849 to a 34-year head keeper, and the 1913 storm, with a Life-Saving station nearby.

light.characteristic: Fl(2) W 20s (ENC record). LighthouseFriends says a flash every ten seconds from 1873; the county's 2014 post says flashes every two minutes. Current characteristic not confirmed from a source read.

lens.where: Original third-order Fresnel installed 1857 (USLHS); the current optic is a DCB 224 aero beacon (USLHS). LighthouseFriends dates the Fresnel's removal to 1969; the county says 1950.

structures.note: First tower, 65 ft, nine lamps in 14-inch reflectors (LighthouseFriends); the county says it stood about 4.5 miles from the point. Replaced by the 1857 tower.
Cylindrical yellow-brick tower, 79 ft from base to lantern centre (USLHS; LighthouseFriends); light's focal plane 88-89 ft above water (LighthouseFriends; USLHS 89 ft)

access.note: USLHS record: open to public. A 2014 county post said the light station is not open to the general public; the 2026 museum season page describes self-guided tower climbs. Check before visiting.

visit.note: Museum and gift shop Wednesday to Sunday, 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., in season; tower open for self-guided climbs from May 2026; admission $8 for adults (museum and tower).

facts.agency: U.S. Coast Guard (remote control since 2003 per Huron County); Huron County owns the grounds and tower under a 2003 transfer from the Bureau of Land Management (LighthouseFriends).

events.note: 65-ft tower constructed and equipped with nine lamps (LighthouseFriends)
Peter L. Shook appointed first keeper, 3 March 1848
LighthouseFriends says Shook likely placed the light in operation at the opening of navigation that year; the USLHS record gives 1847
Catherine Shook appointed after her husband drowned on 31 March 1849 (LighthouseFriends)
New yellow-brick tower linked to a dwelling by a covered passage (LighthouseFriends; USLHS)
Original third-order Fresnel lens (USLHS record)
Fixed white light first exhibited with the opening of navigation in spring 1858 (LighthouseFriends)
Third-order Henry-Lepaute Fresnel lens installed, giving a white flash every ten seconds (LighthouseFriends)
Oil house provided for the station (Lighthouse Board report)
Fog-signal apparatus contracted for and reported completed and ready for inspection (Lighthouse Board report)
Second keeper's dwelling; work began May 1908 and was completed three months later (LighthouseFriends; act of 26 February 1907)
Great Lakes storm of November 1913; snow hid the light by midday Sunday, 9 November (Pointe aux Barques Maritime Museum); Richards tied up the wick (LighthouseFriends, citing a son's recollection)
Gas and whistling buoy No. 1 at Pointe aux Barques not found after the storm (Bulletin)
Illuminant changed from oil to incandescent oil vapor, 28 June 1914
Light electrified; candlepower raised (LighthouseFriends; county blog)
Coast Guard took control of the lights; Richards retired as head keeper in June 1939
Light made unwatched, per Coast Guard Light Lists quoted by LighthouseFriends. The USLHS record gives automation in 1958.
Original Fresnel lens replaced with rotating DCB-224 aero beacons, per the county blog. LighthouseFriends dates removal of the third-order lens to 1969.
Property sold to Huron County for use as a park (LighthouseFriends)
Third-order Henry-Lepaute Fresnel lens removed; donated to Harbor Beach
Volunteers clean up the lighthouse; Pointe aux Barques Lighthouse Society formed
Light transferred from the Bureau of Land Management to Huron County (June 2003); remotely controlled by the Coast Guard from 2003
New cedar roof and brick chimneys on the keeper's dwelling
Coast Guard recovered the third-order lens after a federal court settlement (31 May 2013) and returned it to the lighthouse later that summer (LighthouseFriends)

corrections.proposed: tower, brick, built 1857 (present tower), 24.1 m (79 ft base to lantern centre); the 27.0 m figure is the light's height above water (89 ft, USLHS), not the tower's height
corrections.why: The USLHS record itself gives 'Year Tower Established: 1857' and '79 FT' from base to lantern centre, and '89 FT ABOVE WATER' for the light. LighthouseFriends dates the 1847-48 tower separately (65 ft).

corrections.proposed: 1858 first_lit (spring 1858, first showing from the 1857 tower)
corrections.why: LighthouseFriends describes the 1857 tower being built and first exhibited in spring 1858. No second tower is described in the sources read.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: USLHS gives 1847 ('Year Established'); LighthouseFriends has Shook appointed 3 March 1848 and says he likely placed the light in operation at the opening of navigation that year. The first lighting date is not settled by a source read.

USLHS: 79 ft from base to lantern centre and 89 ft above water. LighthouseFriends: 79 ft tower and a focal plane of 88 ft. The county's 2014 post gives 89 ft, which is the height above water, not the tower. Resolved as 79 ft tower, about 89 ft focal height.

The record gives 1973-03-20. The county's 2014 post says the tower has been registered since 1972. The NRHP nomination (reference 73000949) is not digitized in the cache, so the listing date is not confirmed.

LighthouseFriends says the third-order lens was removed in 1969; the county says the original lens was replaced in 1950 with aero beacons, and that the original beacon's lens is on display at the Huron City Museum. LighthouseFriends says a recovered lens was returned to the light in 2013. USLHS gives the current optic as DCB 224.

LighthouseFriends, citing Light Lists, says unwatched in 1941. USLHS gives 'Year Automated: 1958'. The county says the light has been remotely controlled by the Coast Guard since 2003. The dates can be read as stages (unwatched 1941, automation recorded 1958, remote control 2003); the sources do not say so.

notes_for_editor: Checked 2026-10-22 against page images. LHB 1893 oil-house entry: scan 213 (printed 156), verified. LHB 1899 entry 184: scan 218 (printed 167), not 219 as first cited; verified. LSS 1878 horses passage: scan 106 (printed 103), verified. LSS 1884 heavy-fog entry: scan 272 (printed 267), not 273. LSS 1888 Mona: the 'September 10-15' entry is scan 105 (printed 100); the 'broke up on the 23d' sentence is scan 106 (printed 101). The 1888 vessel-mention citation is NOT a wreck list: scan 52 (printed 47) is the Women's National Relief Association paragraph, which names the schooner Mona at the Pointe aux Barques Station on 10 September 1887 among the cases its stores aided. Corpus scan numbers for these volumes ran one leaf high; corrected from the images. Conflicts stated in the story: 1847 vs 1848 first lighting; 3 March 1847 (LighthouseFriends) vs 3 July 1847 (county blog) for the second $5,000; tower shape (USLHS conical; county cylindrical; LighthouseFriends decagonal lantern); dwelling (county two-level house; LighthouseFriends one-and-a-half-story); tower height (79 ft tower vs 89 ft county); lens dates (1950 county vs 1969 LighthouseFriends); end of resident keepers (1941, 1958, 2003). The Board's 1899 entry says 'Pointe aux Barques, Lake Huron'; the Manistique 'Pointe aux Barques' proposal in the 1891-1901 reports is a different station and is not used. The county's 2014 blog has errors (it gives the Life-Saving station's date as 1976; LighthouseFriends gives 1876); the county's 'Point of Small Boats' translation differs from LighthouseFriends' 'Point of the Little Ships'. The 2005 dwelling restoration comes from LighthouseFriends only. The Maritime Museum storm essay is a member's essay (Glen Willis); cited for the snow scene and attributed as such. The NRHP nomination (reference 73000949) is 'not yet digitized' in the cache. Chronicling America returned unrelated OCR hits for Richards; no newspapers cited. Wikipedia not used. The Homans passage is a LighthouseFriends quotation of an 1838 Navy report that was not read directly. The Charles Kimball link to the roster is by name and date only (probable; the Bulletin gives no middle initial).
